A language model writes one token at a time. To choose the next token it runs every layer of the network over the text so far, and each attention layer compares the newest token with all the tokens before it. Done naively, the work for one token grows with the length of the text, and the work for a whole reply grows with its square. The key-value cache removes the repetition. The keys and values that attention computes for a token depend only on that token and the ones before it, so they never change once they are computed. A runtime stores them, layer by layer, and each new token computes only its own query, key, and value and reads the rest from the cache. The price is memory: the cache holds two vectors per token, per layer, per key-value head, and for a long conversation that is gigabytes. Grouped-query attention makes it smaller by sharing each key-value head among several query heads, which is why the cache is kept at the width of the key-value heads and expanded only when it is used. Position information has to survive the cache as well. With rotary position embeddings a key is rotated by an angle that depends on its position, once, when it is computed, and stored rotated. A new token is rotated for its own position, which is the number of tokens already in the cache, not zero. Runtimes differ in how they store the cache. Some append a slice per token, some reserve room for the whole context in advance, and some keep it in fixed-size blocks so that many requests can share one pool of memory. All of them give the same tokens as the naive loop, only faster. This is why the first token of a reply is slow and the rest are quick: reading the prompt fills the cache for hundreds of tokens at once, and after that each step handles a single token. It is also why a server can keep the cache of a conversation and continue it when the next message arrives, instead of reading everything again.
